meta.title: String Stars in Anti de Sitter Space
meta.abstractHtml: We study the ‘string star’ saddle, also known as the Horowitz-Polchinski solution, in the middle of dimensional thermal AdS space. We show that there’s a regime of temperatures in which the saddle is very similar to the flat space solution found by Horowitz and Polchinski. This saddle is hypothetically connected at lower temperatures to the small AdS black hole saddle. We also study, numerically and analytically, how the solutions are changed due to the AdS geometry for higher temperatures. Specifically, we describe how the solution joins with the thermal gas phase, and find the leading correction to the Hagedorn temperature due to the AdS curvature. Finally, we study the thermodynamic instabilities of the solution and argue for a Gregory-Laflamme-like instability whenever extra dimensions are present at the AdS curvature scale.

children.title: Abstract
children.body: We study the ‘string star’ saddle, also known as the Horowitz-Polchinski solution, in the middle of dimensional thermal AdS space. We show that there’s a regime of temperatures in which the saddle is very similar to the flat space solution found by Horowitz and Polchinski. This saddle is hypothetically connected at lower temperatures to the small AdS black hole saddle. We also study, numerically and analytically, how the solutions are changed due to the AdS geometry for higher temperatures. Specifically, we describe how the solution joins with the thermal gas phase, and find the leading correction to the Hagedorn temperature due to the AdS curvature. Finally, we study the thermodynamic instabilities of the solution and argue for a Gregory-Laflamme-like instability whenever extra dimensions are present at the AdS curvature scale.

children.body: One of the important standing goals in quantum gravity is to understand the microstructure of black holes. As a microscopic theory of quantum gravity, different attempts were made to employ string theory to study the microscopic properties of black holes (for reviews see for example [1, 2]). One such path is the “correspondence principle" [3, 4]. The basic observation is that when one adiabatically shrinks a black hole horizon to the string scale, its thermodynamic properties are qualitatively the same as a generic string state with the same energy [5, 6]. A canonical version of the correspondence principle was offered in [7] in terms of the thermal string theory partition function on (asymptotically) (see also [8, 9, 10, 11, 12, 13, 14]). For near-Hagedorn temperatures , the first string winding mode around the thermal circle is parametrically lighter than the string scale. Upon compactifying the thermal circle, the authors found a ( dimensional) bound state solution of the winding scalar together with gravity. This solution seems to describe a self-gravitating bound state of hot strings. We will call this solution a “string star”. The Euclidean Schwarzschild black hole is another saddle that contributes to the thermal partition function. 1 The solution is perturbative only for large horizons, when the temperature is low enough, . As a result, at generic intermediate temperatures both the black hole and the string star descriptions fail. A naive extrapolation from the perturbative regimes to surprisingly shows a qualitative agreement on the thermodynamic properties between the two saddles. The conclusion might be that thermodynamically, the string star and the black hole are two continuously connected phases. Recently [14] gave an extended and modern outlook on the string star solution, including an analysis from the worldsheet perspective. Below we will follow their conventions.

gist.html: A string-scale black hole and a self-gravitating bound state of hot strings, the string star, may be connected phases.

children.title: The thermal circle and the Hagedorn temperature
children.body: A thermal partition function $\operatorname{Tr}e^{-\beta H}$ is a Euclidean path integral with time periodic, of length $\beta=1/T$: space times a thermal circle. A closed string can wrap this circle. The wrapped string's mass squared is its stretching energy, which grows with the circle's radius $R$, minus a zero-point energy. On a small enough circle, at a high enough temperature, the zero-point term wins and the wrapped string is tachyonic. The radius $R_H$ at which it is massless defines the Hagedorn temperature, beyond which the canonical partition function of a gas of strings diverges, a sign of the exponential growth of the number of string states with energy. Just colder than this temperature, for $R-R_H\ll l_s$, the wrapped string is a light scalar field $\chi$ in the theory reduced on the circle, with $m^2\propto R-R_H$. The string star is a bound state of this light field with gravity.

In this work we study the thermodynamic properties of the string star solution in the middle of thermal anti de Sitter space (AdS), termed the “AdS string star”. This solution should be understood as a saddle that contributes to the string theory partition function on asymptotically (Euclidean) AdS. This partition function also has a (well known) Euclidean AdS Schwarzschild solution called the AdS black hole. We will argue below that a similar “correspondence principle" can be qualitatively drawn between the two Euclidean AdS saddles.2 Studying string theory on AdS has two main advantages. First, the thermal partition function in asymptotically flat space is an ill defined concept in quantum gravity in general, and also in string theory [23]. The AdS partition function on the other hand is well defined, where the radius of the thermal circle is held fixed only at the conformal boundary of space. As a result, the partition function is not strictly thermal in the bulk. The second advantage is that string theory on AdS is holographically dual to a (strongly coupled) conformal field theory (CFT) in one dimension lower [24]. Instead of an ill defined thermal partition function, the AdS partition function is well defined and equals the thermal partition function of the dual CFT.

gist.html: AdS is a better home for the string star: its partition function is well defined and equals a dual CFT's.

But for and close enough to the origin, the winding mode of the string on the thermal circle is light. In this regime we can follow [7] and dimensionally reduce on the time direction. children.body: In figure 1 we schematically plotted the phase diagram of string theory on (asymptotically) thermal as a function of the temperature (see also section 2.3). The thermal AdS saddle, or the thermal gas phase, (in gray) dominates the canonical ensemble at low temperatures. At high temperatures AdS black holes solutions (in black) exist in two branches, “large” and “small”. The large AdS black hole dominates the canonical ensemble at temperatures above the Hawking-Page temperature [26, 27, 28]. The small AdS black hole is always metastable. Its size gets smaller with the temperature such that for the solution is approximately a dimensional Schwarzschild black hole. As we said above, an AdS string star solution (in blue) exists for , and is approximately the flat space solution for low temperatures in this range. Therefore the extrapolation of the AdS string star and the small AdS black hole to follows exactly the flat space analysis of [7]. We find the same qualitative agreement here between the two AdS phases. At higher temperatures the string star’s amplitude goes to zero and the solution smoothly joins with the thermal gas phase at . Note that in this regime of temperatures the gas, the string star and the small AdS black hole are all metastable phases of the canonical ensemble. The small AdS black hole saddle is also known to be thermodynamically unstable [29], and in particular suffers from a Gregory-Laflamme (GL) instability due to the full dimensional geometry [30, 31, 32]. In section 6 we give evidence that the AdS string star is also thermodynamically unstable, and has a GL-like instability.

gist.html: Matching flat space when cold, the star agrees qualitatively with the small AdS black hole; it also has a GL-like instability.

children.title: Black holes in AdS and the Hawking–Page transition
children.body: In anti de Sitter space of radius $l_{ads}$, the Euclidean partition function at temperature $1/\beta$ receives contributions from thermal AdS and from AdS-Schwarzschild black holes. For every $\beta$ below $2\pi l_{ads}/\sqrt{d(d-2)}$ there are two black holes. The large one has a horizon bigger than $l_{ads}$ and positive specific heat; above the Hawking–Page temperature, of order $1/l_{ads}$, its free energy is lower than thermal AdS's, so it dominates. This is the Hawking–Page transition. The small black hole has a horizon smaller than $l_{ads}$ and behaves like a flat-space Schwarzschild black hole, with negative specific heat and positive free energy, so it never dominates. By holography these saddles are phases of the dual CFT on a sphere: thermal AdS is the confined phase, with free energy of order one, and the large black hole the deconfined phase, with free energy of order $N^2$. The small black hole is a metastable phase whose fate at the string scale is the paper's concern.

String stars in flat space exist only for [7]. In AdS on the other hand string star solutions exist close to at every . For the solution turns unreliable as one decreases the temperature to the flat space Hagedorn temperature , and it does not exist for lower temperatures. Numerical extrapolation of its thermodynamics properties shows a qualitative agreement with the small AdS black hole (see section 7). This is a version of the correspondence principle that exists only in AdS.

gist.html: Unlike flat space, AdS string stars exist near $\beta_c$ for every $d$, giving an AdS-only correspondence for $d\ge6$.

children.body: It is useful to understand the phase diagram of figure 1 in terms of the holographic dual CFT. The thermal gas phase in the bulk is associated with the confined phase in the CFT, and the large AdS black hole with the deconfined phase [27, 28]. In the CFT at zero coupling, the two phases meet at the Hagedorn temperature without any further metastable phase, such as the small AdS black hole [33, 34]. At weak coupling there is an intermediate phase with an eigenvalue distribution that is non-uniform but ungapped, and higher loop computations are required to see if it is thermodynamically dominant [34]. One can conjecture [35] that this phase is continuously connected to a string star. In any case at strong coupling it is natural to expect the small AdS black hole phase to connect the large AdS black hole (deconfined) phase at high temperatures to the gas (confined) phase at low temperatures [34]. Here we follow the speculation that this phase turns into a string star around before joining the confined phase, and study the latter behavior. In those terms, this work offers predictions on the connection of this metastable phase to the confined phase at strong coupling. Besides the value of the critical temperature , we also find that the free energy close to is (see section 5). This is the same scaling found in weak coupling [34], and it was expected on general grounds also for strong coupling [35].

gist.html: For the dual CFT the star predicts how a metastable phase meets the confined one, with $F\sim(\beta-\beta_c)^2$.

children.title: The Hagedorn transition in weakly coupled gauge theory
children.body: A weakly coupled large-$N$ gauge theory on a sphere can be reduced to a matrix model for the holonomy $U$ of the gauge field around the thermal circle, by integrating out all other modes. In the confined phase the eigenvalues of $U$ are spread uniformly around the circle and $u_1=\operatorname{Tr}U/N$, the Polyakov loop, vanishes. At the Hagedorn temperature the coefficient of $|u_1|^2$ in the effective action changes sign, and the uniform distribution becomes unstable. Near that point the effective action is $a\,\delta T\,|u_1|^2+b\,|u_1|^4$, whose extremum away from $u_1=0$ is a phase with a non-uniform but ungapped eigenvalue distribution, and free energy scaling as $\delta T^2$. Whether this phase is stable depends on the sign of $b$, which needs higher-loop computations. Following it further, the distribution develops a gap through a third-order Gross–Wadia–Witten transition. At strong coupling the analogous branch is expected to be the small AdS black hole, and the paper's string star reproduces the $\delta T^2$ scaling of the free energy.

Even if the string star and the black hole are two continuously connected phases, a high order phase transition can still occur between them. In [14] it was argued, using worldsheet methods, that in flat space type IIB a phase transition between the string star and the black hole is necessary. It would be interesting to see if similar arguments can be used directly in AdS as well. We can also consider these saddles in type IIB on using the analysis of this work. The transition between the two happens in our setting when the two phases are ignorant of the AdS geometry, and thus the argument from [14] follows. This theory is holographic to super Yang-Mills, in which a third order Gross-Wadia-Witten phase transition was shown for the metastable phase in weak coupling [34]. If this phase transition follows to strong coupling, as conjectured by [35, 36], it might be the same phase transition advocated in [14].

gist.html: A phase transition may still separate star and black hole; in $AdS_5\times S^5$ it might be Gross–Wadia–Witten's.

children.body: More broadly, one may hope to find the states corresponding to the AdS string star in the holographic CFT. At this point it seems very hard, first of all because the holographic CFT is strongly coupled. Also, this phase has no clear order parameter that distinguishes it from any other generic state at those temperatures. As a first step, further work can find the (qualitative) expectation value of a Polyakov loop (as a function of the temperature ) in this phase compared to the other Euclidean saddles.

gist.html: Finding the star's states in the strongly coupled CFT looks hard; a Polyakov loop would be a first step.
In AdS the string star matches flat space when cold, joins the gas at a shifted Hagedorn temperature, and is unstable.

brief.html: A string-scale black hole and a self-gravitating ball of hot strings, the string star, agree in rough thermodynamics, so they may be one phase. The paper builds the string star at the centre of thermal AdS, where the partition function is well defined and holographic. Cold, it is the flat-space star, and so matches the small AdS black hole; hotter, its size is bounded and it joins the thermal gas at the AdS Hagedorn temperature. It exists there in every dimension, and offers the dual CFT strong-coupling predictions.

children.title: The Gregory–Laflamme instability
children.body: A black string, a black hole extended along a direction much longer than its horizon radius $r_h$, is classically unstable: perturbations varying along the string as $e^{ikz}$, with $k$ below a critical value of order $1/r_h$, grow exponentially in time (Gregory and Laflamme, 1993). Thermodynamics anticipates this: when the direction is compact and long, a black hole localized in all directions has more entropy than the uniform string of the same mass. In the Euclidean picture the threshold mode is static, a zero mode of the action, and the longer-wavelength ones are negative modes, inherited from the negative mode of the lower-dimensional black hole. A small AdS black hole in $AdS_5\times S^5$ is such a black string smeared over the $S^5$; when its horizon is much smaller than $l_{ads}$ it is unstable towards a black hole localized on the sphere, a ten-dimensional black hole. The paper looks for the same structure, the Gregory–Laflamme instability, in the string star.

gist.html: The star's free energy is positive, so it never dominates; it and the small black hole both fail near $\beta\sim l_s$.

children.title: The Horowitz–Polchinski solution
children.body: For the Horowitz–Polchinski solution, Horowitz and Polchinski reduced string theory on the thermal circle just below the Hagedorn temperature, keeping the light winding scalar $\chi$, with $m^2\propto(R-R_H)/R_H$ in string units, and the Newtonian potential $\varphi$, the fluctuation of the circle's size. Because the winding mass falls where the circle shrinks, $\chi$ sources a negative $\varphi$, which lowers its own mass: the condensate attracts itself. A bound state exists when this attraction balances the gradient and mass terms. Scaling the equations, the solution has size $L\sim l_s((R-R_H)/R_H)^{-1/2}$, amplitude of order $(R-R_H)/R_H$, and entropy of order $(l_s^{d-1}/G_N)((R-R_H)/R_H)^{(4-d)/2}$. Normalizable solutions exist only for $3\le d\le5$ spatial dimensions. Extrapolated to $R-R_H\sim l_s$, the size and entropy match those of a string-sized black hole: the correspondence principle in canonical form. The paper's cold AdS star is this solution.

children.body: In this section we will study the thermodynamic stability of the solutions we found. As we reviewed in section 2.3 above (and plotted in figure 1), the free energy of the string star is positive, and thus larger than both the gas (thermal AdS) and the large black hole saddles. This phase is therefore canonically unstable. As these phases are different Euclidean saddles for small , this instability is non-perturbative in .

gist.html: With positive free energy the star is non-perturbatively unstable towards the gas and the large black hole.

children.body: At higher temperatures we hope the string star is continuously connected to the Euclidean saddle of a small AdS black hole. The latter is a well defined Euclidean saddle only for temperatures . Just like the string star solution, this phase is also subdominant compared to the large AdS black hole and the gas phases. But apart from these non-perturbative instabilities, the small AdS black hole also has a perturbative instability: the quadratic variation matrix of the solution’s Euclidean action has a normalizable negative eigenmode [29]. The negative mode is related to the fact this phase also has negative specific heat. Negative specific heat is yet another sort of thermodynamic instability. But for black holes one can show it is actually related to the negative eigenmode [42]. Intuitively the specific heat is related to the (quadratic) decrease of the free energy when changing the size of the black hole. The negative mode of [29] exactly changes (off-shell) the size of the black hole on the spatial metric components. The decrease of the free-energy at second order by the temperature (due to negative specific heat) is then mapped to the second variation of this normalizable mode.

gist.html: The small AdS black hole also has a Euclidean negative mode, tied to its negative specific heat.

children.title: Negative modes of Euclidean saddles
children.body: Around a saddle of the Euclidean action, the path integral is approximated by a Gaussian integral over fluctuations, weighted by the second variation of the action. If that second variation has a negative eigenvalue on a normalizable fluctuation, a negative mode, the Gaussian integral diverges and must be defined by rotating the contour; the saddle then gives the free energy an imaginary part, the signature of an instability, as a bounce does for tunnelling. Gross, Perry and Yaffe found such a mode for the Euclidean Schwarzschild black hole: a change of the horizon size at fixed asymptotic temperature. It is tied to the black hole's negative specific heat, since the free energy at fixed temperature is then a maximum rather than a minimum in the black hole's size. A thermodynamically stable saddle has no negative mode. The paper asks whether the string star has one.

Does the string star have such a negative mode as well? For the flat space string star it was shown in [7, 14] that such a mode exists. As a result, such a mode exists also in AdS, whenever we trust the flat space approximation (3.3). We believe that such a negative mode exists also for higher temperatures, although we couldn’t find a general argument. Somewhat similar to the black hole saddle, close to the AdS Hagedorn temperature we can use the specific heat to argue for the existence of such a negative mode. The string star solution to (2.7) implicitly depends on through the equations’ dependence on . children.body: The last type of instability we will consider has to do with the full ten dimensional geometry. We assumed our full geometry is (asymptotically ) , where is compact with the characteristic size (the AdS curvature scale). Before explaining the instability of the string star phase, we turn again to the small AdS black hole saddle. This time, we start by considering the Lorentzian solution. In terms of the dimensional geometry, this solution is homogeneous along the directions. When the AdS black hole horizon is much smaller than the size of the compact direction there’s a classical mode of the spatial dimensional metric, modulated around the coordinates, that grows exponentially with time [31, 32, 43]. This is a classical (or dynamical) instability, that breaks the homogeneity of the solution. It is known as the Gregory-Laflamme (GL) instability [30, 44, 45]. In this way small AdS black holes turn into dimensional black holes [46]. In other words, this is the dynamical manifestation of the dimensional black hole being thermodynamically favored over a small AdS black hole (see section 2.3 and figure 1) [47, 48, 49]. The relation between the two instabilities however is so far indirect, as we just described a Lorentzian and classical instability, and in thermodynamics we consider Euclidean saddles and the off-shell modes around them. Nevertheless the relation can be shown more rigorously. The dynamical modes are eventually equivalent to dimensional Euclidean negative modes, and both are related to the same negative mode of the ( dimensional) small AdS black hole that we mentioned at the beginning of the section [50, 51, 49, 42, 31, 44]. The basic idea is that for high enough frequency along the time exponent turns to zero. At that point we have a stationary solution that can be trivially Wick-rotated to a zero mode of the Euclidean dimensional solution. Thinking of the kinetic energy on as a linear source, this mode also describes a negative (off-shell) mode in Euclidean dimensions.

gist.html: Small AdS black holes suffer a Gregory–Laflamme instability towards ten-dimensional ones, tied to their Euclidean negative mode.

In the Euclidean setting however, we can still ask whether there are negative dimensional modes of the solution. Similar to the small AdS black hole saddle, these modes are related to the dimensional negative mode discussed at the beginning of the section, as we will show now.

children.title: Holographic entanglement entropy
children.body: For a state of a holographic CFT and a region $A$ of space, Ryu and Takayanagi proposed that the entanglement entropy of $A$ is the area of the extremal bulk surface $X$ ending on the boundary of $A$, divided by $4G_N$. Lewkowycz and Maldacena derived this from the replica trick: $\operatorname{Tr}\rho_A^n$ is the action of a bulk saddle whose boundary has $n$ copies glued along $A$, and as $n\to1$ the variation of that action localizes on $X$. Faulkner, Lewkowycz and Maldacena added the first quantum correction, the entanglement entropy of the bulk fields in the region $a$ between $X$ and $A$, of order one rather than $1/G_N$. For bulk matter in a thermal state, that term is the matter's thermal entropy in $a$. The paper reads its holographic entanglement entropy this way: the string star's thermal entropy, of order $1/G_N$, adds to the area term.

brief.html:
A black hole shrunk to the string scale has roughly the thermodynamics of a string state of the same energy: the “correspondence principle”. In Horowitz and Polchinski's canonical version, the string wound around the Euclidean time circle, light just below the Hagedorn temperature, binds with gravity into a “string star”. The paper places this star at the centre of thermal anti de Sitter space, where the partition function is well defined and equals that of a dual CFT. When cold, the AdS star is the flat-space one, so its rough agreement with a string-sized black hole carries over; when hotter, it fades into the thermal gas. It does so at the AdS Hagedorn temperature, which the paper computes, with scalings that give the dual CFT strong-coupling predictions.

In thermal AdS the time circle widens away from the centre. The winding string's mass is set by the local radius, so it is light only near the centre, and near the flat-space Hagedorn radius $R_H$. Reducing on the circle gives an effective theory in $d$ spatial dimensions for the winding mode $\chi$ and the circle's size $\varphi$; its bound states are the AdS string stars. A star much smaller than $\sqrt{l_sl_{ads}}$ does not feel the curvature and solves exactly the Horowitz–Polchinski equations. With $R_0$ the circle's radius at the centre (larger is colder), this holds for $l_s/l_{ads}\ll(R_0-R_H)/R_H\ll1$, and only for $3\le d\le5$. At the cold end of this window the star is string-sized, with entropy $S\sim l_s^{d-1}/G_N$, like a string-sized small AdS black hole. Both are far smaller than the AdS radius, so the flat-space comparison carries over. Their holographic entanglement entropies agree in the same way.

Hotter, at $R_H$, the winding mass vanishes at the centre but grows as $\rho^2$ away from it, a confining potential, so the star keeps a size of order $\sqrt{l_sl_{ads}}$ instead of diverging. Hotter still, the paper assumes, and its numerics support, that the star loses amplitude until it merges with thermal AdS at a critical radius $R_c$, below $R_H$. Near the merger the amplitude grows as $(R_0-R_c)^{1/2}$ and the free energy as $(R_0-R_c)^2$, the scaling found in the weakly coupled dual gauge theory. Since this analysis holds in any dimension, AdS string stars exist near $R_c$ for every $d$. For $d\ge6$ numerics show them shrinking to string size near $R_H$, with the entropy of a string-sized black hole: a correspondence that exists only in AdS.

At the merger thermal AdS has a normalizable zero mode, so $R_c$ is where the string gas turns tachyonic: the AdS Hagedorn temperature. Near the centre the linearized equation is a harmonic oscillator, and the zero mode is its ground state. Its zero-point energy must be paid by a negative mass squared at the centre, so the gas becomes unstable hotter than in flat space. To leading order $R_c/R_H=1-\frac{d}{\sqrt{2\kappa}}\frac{l_s}{l_{ads}}$, with $\kappa$ a constant of the string theory. For type IIB on $AdS_5\times S^5$ this gives N=4 super Yang–Mills a Hagedorn temperature $T_c=\lambda^{1/4}/\sqrt{8\pi^2}+1/2\pi$ at strong coupling. Its constant agrees with integrability numerics.

With positive free energy, the star is subdominant to the gas and the large black hole. It also appears to have a negative mode, a fluctuation that lowers its Euclidean action. It is inherited from flat space in the cold window, and near $R_c$ follows from the star's negative specific heat. For $3\le d\le5$ the paper suggests the two are one mode, present throughout. When the compact part of space has the AdS size, such a mode, modulated along it, stays negative, except too close to $R_c$. This is the string star's analogue of the Gregory–Laflamme instability that turns small AdS black holes ten-dimensional.

The link to the small AdS black hole remains a qualitative extrapolation: neither saddle is reliable near $\beta\sim l_s$, and whether they connect is open, as in flat space. Between $R_H$ and $R_c$ no analytic solution is known, and the smooth merger with the gas is the simplest scenario, checked numerically. Too close to $R_c$ one-loop effects dominate the tree-level free energy. The negative mode is shown only near the two ends of the temperature range, and what the star decays into is open. Nor are the star's states identified in the dual CFT.

defs.html: A self-gravitating bound state of hot strings: a condensate of the string wound around the Euclidean time circle, held together by the gravity it sources (Horowitz and Polchinski). It exists near the Hagedorn temperature; the “AdS string star” is the paper's version, at the centre of thermal AdS.

The Euclidean time direction, periodic because a thermal trace is a path integral on a circle of length $\beta=1/T$. In thermal AdS it widens away from the centre; the paper labels temperatures by its radius at the centre, $R_0=\beta/2\pi$, so larger $R_0$ is colder.

at.quote: the circumference of the thermal circle

defs.html: Euclidean anti de Sitter space with periodic time and no black hole, of topology $R^d\times S^1$. It is the saddle of the thermal gas phase, and its on-shell action is set to zero here, the reference for every other saddle.

A classical solution of the Euclidean gravitational action with the given boundary conditions, such as thermal AdS, a black hole or the string star. To leading order each contributes $e^{-I}$ to the partition function, $I$ being its on-shell action, and each is a possible phase.

The temperature at which, in flat space, the string wound once around the thermal circle becomes massless: $\beta_H=2\pi R_H$, with $R_H=\sqrt2\,l_s$ for type II. Hotter, that mode is tachyonic and a gas of strings is unstable. In AdS the paper finds it shifted, to the AdS Hagedorn temperature.

The temperature above which the thermal gas in AdS turns tachyonic, $\beta_c=2\pi R_c$, slightly hotter than the flat-space value because the curvature confines the winding mode. The string star's amplitude vanishes there and it merges with the gas; holographically it is the dual CFT's Hagedorn temperature.

The phase described by thermal AdS: a gas of particles and strings at the boundary's temperature, with no black hole. It dominates at low temperatures and corresponds to the confined phase of the dual CFT. The string star merges with it at the AdS Hagedorn temperature.

at.quote: joins with the thermal gas phase

defs.html: The branch of AdS black holes whose horizon shrinks as the temperature rises, with $r_h\approx(d-2)\beta/4\pi$ when much smaller than the AdS radius. It has negative specific heat and never dominates; at the string scale it is the black hole the string star might continue into.

at.quote: small AdS black holes decay into

defs.html: The Gregory–Laflamme instability: a black hole or black string smeared along a compact direction much larger than its horizon is unstable to perturbations varying along it, and clumps. Small AdS black holes in $AdS_5\times S^5$ suffer it along the sphere and become ten-dimensional black holes.

The observation (Susskind; Horowitz and Polchinski) that a black hole shrunk to the string scale has, up to factors of order one, the entropy of a typical string state of the same mass. It suggests a black hole may turn smoothly into strings, though both descriptions fail at the matching point.

The length $l_s=\sqrt{\alpha'}$ set by the string tension, below which strings cannot be treated as particles. The effective theory holds for solutions much larger than $l_s$; the paper assumes $l_s\ll l_{ads}$ and computes numerically in string units, $l_s=1$.

The string state wound once around the thermal circle, a scalar field $\chi$ after reduction on the circle. Its mass squared grows with the local circle radius and vanishes at the Hagedorn radius, so near that temperature it is light and can condense into a string star.

The radius $l_{ads}$ of anti de Sitter space. The paper assumes it much larger than the string length, and the ratio $l_s/l_{ads}$ controls every correction. For type IIB on $AdS_5\times S^5$, $(l_{ads}/l_s)^4=\lambda$, the 't Hooft coupling of the dual gauge theory.

The solution with no winding condensate and no backreaction, $\chi=\varphi=0$: thermal AdS itself, the gas phase. The string star merges with it at the AdS Hagedorn temperature, where the trivial solution has a zero mode.

The size of the string star's fields: the value of the winding mode $\chi$, and of the circle's fluctuation $\varphi$, at the centre. The effective theory needs it small; it goes to zero as the temperature approaches the AdS Hagedorn temperature, where the star becomes thermal AdS.

at.quote: amplitude goes to zero and it joins

defs.html: The branch of AdS black holes whose horizon grows with the temperature, exceeding the AdS radius when hot. It dominates the canonical ensemble above the Hawking–Page temperature and corresponds to the deconfined phase of the dual CFT.

at.quote: The large AdS black hole dominates

defs.html: The temperature, of order $1/l_{ads}$, above which the large AdS black hole has lower free energy than thermal AdS and dominates. In the dual CFT it is the confinement–deconfinement transition. It is far colder than the Hagedorn temperature.

Said of the saddle of least free energy, which gives the leading contribution to the partition function at small $G_N$; the others are exponentially suppressed, or subdominant. The string star never dominates.

at.quote: dominates the canonical ensemble at low temperatures

defs.html: Said of a saddle that is a valid solution but has higher free energy than another, so it contributes subleadingly to the partition function. Near the Hagedorn temperature the gas, the string star and the small AdS black hole are all metastable.

at.quote: The small AdS black hole is always metastable

defs.html: The low-temperature phase of a large-$N$ gauge theory on a sphere, whose free energy is of order one rather than $N^2$ and whose Polyakov loop vanishes. Holographically it is the thermal gas in AdS; the deconfined phase, the large black hole, takes over when hot.

at.quote: associated with the confined phase in the CFT

defs.html: A third-order transition of large-$N$ unitary matrix models, at which the eigenvalue distribution of the matrix, here the Polyakov loop's holonomy, develops a gap. In weakly coupled $\mathcal N=4$ super Yang–Mills it occurs in the metastable phase near the Hagedorn temperature.

The trace of the holonomy of the gauge field around the thermal circle. In a large-$N$ gauge theory on a sphere its expectation value vanishes in the confined phase and not in the deconfined one, so it serves as an order parameter.

at.quote: expectation value of a Polyakov loop

defs.html: The radius over which the string star's winding mode decays: its size. Numerically, where $\chi$ has fallen by $e^{-1/2}$ from its central value. It grows as the temperature rises, diverging at the Hagedorn temperature in flat space but bounded near $\sqrt{l_sl_{ads}}$ in AdS.

at.quote: length scale as a function of the inverse

defs.html: The paper's entropy in units of $l_s^{d-1}\omega_{d-1}/16\pi G_N$, with $\omega_{d-1}$ the area of the unit sphere, so that $s$ of order one means $S\sim l_s^{d-1}/G_N$, the entropy of a string-sized black hole. The free energy is normalized likewise, as $f$.

A normalizable solution of the linearized equations around a solution: a fluctuation that leaves its action unchanged at second order. Thermal AdS has one exactly at the AdS Hagedorn temperature, where the string star branches off it; hotter, that mode is tachyonic.

at.quote: the trivial solution has a zero mode

defs.html: The string star's size at the AdS Hagedorn temperature, $L_c^2=\sqrt{2/\kappa}\,l_sl_{ads}$: the width of the Gaussian zero mode of thermal AdS there. It bounds the AdS string star's size and is much smaller than the AdS radius.

at.quote: The critical length scale of the solution

defs.html: A normalizable fluctuation that lowers a Euclidean saddle's action at second order, so that the saddle is not a local minimum: a sign of instability. For black holes it accompanies negative specific heat; the paper argues the string star has one, at least near both ends of its temperature range.

Computing an entanglement entropy from $\operatorname{Tr}\rho_A^n$, the partition function on $n$ copies of space glued along the region $A$, continued in $n$ to $n\to1$. Holographically each such trace is the action of a bulk saddle with replicated boundary conditions.

questions.q: Why study the string star in AdS rather than in flat space?
questions.a: For two reasons the paper gives. A thermal partition function in asymptotically flat space is ill defined in quantum gravity, while in AdS the temperature is fixed only at the boundary and the partition function is well defined. And string theory in AdS is dual to a CFT, so each bulk saddle is a phase of a field theory: the string star becomes a prediction for the strongly coupled CFT near its Hagedorn temperature.

questions.q: What do $\beta$, $R_0$, $R_H$, $R_c$, $\kappa$ and $d$ mean, and which way is hotter?
questions.a: $\beta$ is the length of the thermal circle at the centre of AdS and $R_0=\beta/2\pi$ its radius; larger $R_0$ is colder. $R_H$ is the flat-space Hagedorn radius and $R_c<R_H$ the AdS one, so the star lives from somewhat colder than $R_H$ up to $R_c$. $AdS_{d+1}$ has $d$ spatial dimensions, and $X_{9-d}$ is the compact rest of space. $\kappa$ is the slope of the winding mass at $R_H$: 4 for type II, $4\sqrt2$ for heterotic.

questions.q: Does the string star ever dominate the partition function?
questions.a: No. For the small amplitudes the effective theory needs, its free energy is positive, while thermal AdS has zero and the large black hole negative free energy. It is a metastable saddle, like the small AdS black hole. The paper studies it as the phase that may connect the small black hole to the gas, not as a dominant one.

questions.q: Why does the AdS star stay finite at the flat-space Hagedorn temperature, where the flat-space star grows without bound?
questions.a: Because the winding mass is set by the local radius of the thermal circle, which widens away from the centre. Even when the mass vanishes at the centre, it grows quadratically away from it. This acts as a harmonic potential that confines the condensate to a size of order $\sqrt{l_sl_{ads}}$, the geometric mean of the string and AdS lengths. In flat space nothing confines it, and the size diverges at $R_H$.

questions.q: Why is the AdS Hagedorn temperature higher than the flat-space one?
questions.a: The gas turns unstable when the winding mode gains a normalizable zero mode. In AdS its linearized equation is that of a harmonic oscillator, whose ground state has a positive zero-point energy, $d/L_c^2$. A negative mass squared at the centre must cancel it, and that needs a circle smaller than $R_H$: a higher temperature. The shift is of order $l_s/l_{ads}$.

questions.q: How does the result compare with what is known for $\mathcal N=4$ super Yang–Mills and for $AdS_3$?
questions.a: With $(l_{ads}/l_s)^4=\lambda$ the formula gives $T_c=\lambda^{1/4}/\sqrt{8\pi^2}+1/2\pi+\dots$ Its constant, $0.159\dots$, agrees with the value fitted to numerical integrability results, and the formula was found independently by Maldacena. In $AdS_3$ with NS-NS flux the exact correction is of order $l_s^2/l_{ads}^2$ instead; the paper explains that this flux changes the winding mass, which R-R flux does not.

questions.q: How close to $R_c$ can the classical solution be trusted?
questions.a: Not arbitrarily close. At $R_c$ the tree-level free energy vanishes while a mode becomes massless, so one-loop effects take over: this is the string gas's own Hagedorn instability. Requiring the Euclidean action to stay large gives $(R_0-R_c)/R_c\gg(l_s/l_{ads})^{(d-2)/4}\,g$, a narrow region at weak string coupling $g$.

questions.q: Why do AdS string stars exist for $d\ge6$, when flat-space ones do not?
questions.a: Near the AdS Hagedorn temperature the star grows out of thermal AdS's zero mode, which exists in any dimension because the curvature supplies a confining potential. The flat-space obstruction for $d\ge6$ enters only at lower temperatures. For $d\ge6$ the numerics show the star shrinking to string size near $R_H$, where it stops being reliable, with the entropy of a string-sized black hole: a correspondence only AdS offers.

questions.q: How does a negative specific heat show that the star has a negative mode?
questions.a: The paper takes as trial fluctuation the temperature derivative of the solution, which is normalizable. Its second variation is a positive term, linear in $R_0-R_c$ near $R_c$, plus a term proportional to the specific heat. Near $R_c$ the entropy grows linearly in $R_0-R_c$, so the specific heat is negative and of order one, and it wins: the fluctuation lowers the action.

questions.q: What does a Gregory–Laflamme-like instability mean for a string star, which has no horizon?
questions.a: For the Euclidean star the paper looks not for growing Lorentzian modes but for negative modes of the action that vary along the compact space. A $d$-dimensional negative mode with eigenvalue $\lambda<0$, modulated as $e^{ikz}$ along a compact direction, gains $k^2$, so it stays negative for $k<\sqrt{-\lambda}$. Such modes fit if the compact space, of size $l_{ads}$, is larger than $1/\sqrt{-\lambda}$.

questions.q: What does the unstable string star decay into?
questions.a: The paper leaves this open. The small AdS black hole's Gregory–Laflamme instability ends on a ten-dimensional black hole, but at the string star's temperatures such black holes cannot be trusted, and ten-dimensional flat-space string stars do not seem to exist. It asks whether the star might decay into string-sized ten-dimensional black holes, which may exist near the Hagedorn temperature in large dimensions.

questions.q: How does the string star's entanglement entropy differ from a black hole's?
questions.a: Both have an area term, $\text{Area}(X)/4G_N$. For the black hole the surface is deformed by the horizon; for the star it is nearly that of thermal AdS, and the extra entropy, also of order $1/G_N$, is a matter term: the strings' thermal entropy inside the region. If star and black hole connect continuously, this term should turn into the black hole's area term; a finite-$\alpha'$ formula might show how.

questions.q: What does the paper not show?
questions.a: It does not show that the string star and the small AdS black hole connect: their agreement extrapolates both to $\beta\sim l_s$, where neither is reliable, and a phase transition could still separate them. Between $R_H$ and $R_c$ the smooth merger with the gas is assumed and checked numerically, not derived. The negative mode is argued only near the ends of the temperature range, and the star's states in the dual CFT are not identified.
